design_detail: Review with a stated search and explicit selection criteria (Psychopharmacology 2016;233:3473-3501), read as the PubMed Central full text. One database (PubMed) searched to 14 November 2015 with a PICO-derived string; 88 records found, 33 included after applying inclusion criteria (in vivo imaging of a neurotransmitter system; a comparison group naive to MDMA or a baseline measurement before use) and exclusion criteria (case reports, reviews, single-challenge studies, re-analyses of published data). Data were extracted into tables by receptor or transporter, and the reviewers themselves computed percentage differences and Cohen's d from printed means and standard deviations where possible. No risk-of-bias assessment, no protocol, no meta-analysis.
can_establish: What the molecular imaging literature up to late 2015 contains and how it distributes: which studies measured which marker, in how many people, with which radioligand and after what abstinence, together with the reviewers' own calculations of percentage change and effect size for each comparison, and the authors' count that 14 of 16 human transporter studies found a significant reduction and that human dopamine studies mostly found none.
cannot_establish: Whether the included studies are sound (none was appraised); whether lower binding means neurotoxicity, which the review says repeatedly cannot be settled by imaging; the size of any pooled effect (no meta-analysis); or whether binding recovers within a person, since every 'recovery' study it cites compares different people or different groups at one time.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review of published studies). Participants in the human studies included range, as the review states, from 14 to 116 people per study.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: in vivo imaging findings on a neurotransmitter system, with a comparison group naive to MDMA or a baseline measurement in an MDMA-naive state. Excluded: case reports and reviews, studies giving MDMA as a single challenge, and re-evaluations of previously published data (Methodology, 'Selection of studies').
sample.attrition: Not applicable; the flow from 88 records to 33 included studies is shown only in Figure 1, which is an image and was not read.
sample.selection_effects: One database and no grey literature or registry search, so unpublished null findings cannot enter; the inclusion rule requiring an MDMA-naive comparison excludes within-person designs without a naive baseline.

exposure.measurement: As reported by each included study; the review tabulates the exposure check for every human study (self-report, urine screening, hair analysis) and the minimum abstinence required (Tables 2-10).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Tabulated per study. For context the review states that a Dutch ecstasy tablet contained about 138 mg of MDMA, which it converts to 2-4 mg/kg in a person of 70 kg, and that animal studies used 20-141 mg/kg, mostly twice daily for 4 days, usually intraperitoneally (Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter').
exposure.polysubstance: Treated as a central problem: the review devotes a section to it, concluding from two studies that cannabis, cocaine and hallucinogen use do not appear to change the transporter findings, and showing with a dopamine study that a significant difference against drug-naive controls disappeared against polydrug controls (Discussion, 'MDMA and additional drug use').

comparison.controls: Varies by study: drug-naive controls, polydrug controls who had not used MDMA, or the same people before use.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that almost all human studies are cross-sectional and cannot exclude premorbid differences; only the Dutch prospective cohort had pre-use measurements.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Tabulated per study; the review repeatedly stresses that a polydrug comparison group is needed and that findings can disappear when one is used.

outcomes.instruments: SPECT and PET imaging of the serotonin transporter ([123I]beta-CIT, [11C]McN5652, [11C]DASB, [18F]ADAM), 5-HT2A receptor, 5-HT1A receptor, serotonin synthesis ([11C]AMT), vesicular monoamine transporter, dopamine D2/3 receptor and release, dopamine transporter and decarboxylase activity ([18F]dopa).
outcomes.validity_norms: Discussed at length: the review explains that [123I]beta-CIT binds both the dopamine and serotonin transporter so striatal serotonin binding cannot be assessed with it, that ratio methods are sensitive to tracer delivery, that scanner resolution causes partial-volume underestimation, and that no PET or SPECT tracer measures toxicity directly.
outcomes.operationalization: Change in receptor or transporter binding, expressed as the percentage difference from the control condition and as Cohen's d, both computed by the reviewers from printed means and standard deviations.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no pooling). The review records which primary studies corrected for multiple comparisons and marks those p-values in its tables.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate. Counts: 14 of 16 human transporter studies found a significant loss of binding, with effect sizes from -0.05 to -2.17; 9 of 11 animal studies (the Discussion says 10 of 11), with effect sizes from -0.38 to -20.03. Of 10 human studies measuring occipital cortex, 6 found their largest reduction there (effect sizes -0.21 to -2.17); 3 of 4 found lower hippocampal binding; 11 found lower thalamic binding but only 3 significantly. Five human 5-HT2A studies split 3 increases against 2 decreases. One animal and five human dopamine studies found almost nothing: of three dopamine transporter studies one found a 13% increase against polydrug controls (p=0.045, d=2.92) and the other two no difference; decarboxylase activity was 9% higher in the putamen of people who had stopped than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021, d=1.10) but no different from polydrug controls; dopamine D2/3 binding and release did not differ.
analysis.selective_reporting: The tables report all extracted outcomes per study, including non-significant ones, and mark which p-values were corrected for multiplicity.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the review notes that human studies ranged from 14 to 116 participants and animal studies from 1 to 26 animals.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A tabulation of 33 imaging studies: lower serotonin transporter binding in most human studies of heavier ecstasy use, largest in occipital cortex; inconsistent 5-HT2A findings; and no consistent dopamine effect in humans. Several studies report higher binding in people with longer abstinence, all of them comparing different people or different groups.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that in people abstinent from the drug, significant recovery of transporter binding was found over time, and the 'Current knowledge' box states that after 40 to 200 days transporter binding recovers. The 40 days comes from a baboon study and the 200 days from one cross-sectional extrapolation for the pallidostriatum in a study that found no recovery in neocortex; no study followed people over abstinence. The conclusions elsewhere are careful: the review says repeatedly that imaging cannot show whether lower binding is neurotoxicity, and that it is unclear whether any recovery of binding means functionally intact neurons.

timeline.event: A systematic review of neuroimaging in moderate MDMA use (Mueller et al.) found no convincing evidence of neurotoxicity at moderate doses; this review cites it in its introduction.
A later systematic review and meta-analysis of neurocognitive outcomes after sustained abstinence reaches a different question but overlaps in the primary studies

replication.where_it_stands: The most complete tabulation of molecular imaging in this field that the project has read; it is a catalogue with the reviewers' own effect-size calculations rather than an appraisal, and its headline statements about recovery go beyond the designs it tabulates.

funding.funder: The authors state that they received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Nuclear Medicine and Radiology, Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam. Two of the three authors are authors of several of the included primary studies (the SPECT studies of 2001 and 2008 and the serotonin-synthesis study of 2014), which the review does not flag.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with two databases or more, duplicate screening and extraction, a risk-of-bias instrument applied to the primary studies, and separate synthesis of within-person designs, so that the recovery question is answered from studies that measured the same people twice rather than from cross-sectional comparisons.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (humans and animals exposed to ecstasy or MDMA), intervention, comparison (MDMA-naive group or pre-use baseline) and outcome (in vivo imaging of a neurotransmitter system) are stated in the Methodology.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Animal, human cross-sectional and prospective studies are pooled into the tables without an explanation of the choice of designs.
PubMed only, to 14 November 2015; no second database, no reference-list searching, no grey literature, registries or contact with authors reported.
Not described; the Methodology says only that full-text articles were obtained and criteria applied.
Extracted items are listed but not who extracted them or whether two people did.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only Figure 1, a flow chart, is offered; it is an image that was not read, and no list of excluded studies with reasons appears in the article.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2-11 give technique, author, group sizes, inclusion criteria, exposure check, outcomes and the reviewers' effect sizes; setting, funding, recruitment and the exact dose or abstinence of each group are not consistently given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No instrument is applied; methodological problems are discussed in general terms in the Limitations.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported for any included study.
No pooling; the reviewers compute per-study percentage changes and Cohen's d only.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations discuss sample sizes, washout, tablet purity and uncorrected multiplicity, but with no risk-of-bias assessment the conclusions treat studies as interchangeable, and the counts of significant findings give each study equal weight.
Sources of variation are discussed at length: radioligand selectivity, quantification method, scanner resolution, abstinence, polydrug use, age at first exposure and sex.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The review reports no funding and no conflicts; it does not note that two authors wrote several included studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (no protocol, a one-database search, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment) and publication bias was not investigated. The review is a reliable map of what imaging studies exist and what they reported, and its per-study calculations are useful, but its counts of significant findings carry no weighting by study quality, and its conclusions about recovery go beyond the designs tabulated. Claims may cite it for the shape of the literature and for its own extracted figures, not as evidence for a magnitude.

key_findings.finding: Of 33 included studies, 27 measured the serotonin transporter: 16 in humans, of which 14 found a significant reduction, with effect sizes from -0.05 to -2.17; and 11 in animals, of which the abstract says 9 and the Discussion says 10 were significant, with effect sizes from -0.38 to -20.03.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results; Results, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st paragraph; Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The counts of significant animal studies differ between the abstract (9 of 11) and the Discussion (10 of 11).

key_findings.finding: Of 10 human studies that measured occipital cortex, 6 found their largest reduction there (effect sizes -0.21 to -2.17); 3 of 4 studies found lower hippocampal binding; 11 studies reported lower thalamic binding but only 3 significantly.

The table of human transporter studies records, among others: Kish et al. (2010), 49 against 50 people, hippocampus -31% and occipital -39%; Erritzoe et al. (2011), neocortex -56%, pallidostriatum -19%, amygdala -32%; McCann et al. (2005), occipital -68% with [11C]DASB and -54% with [11C]McN5652; Selvaraj et al. (2009), no difference; de Win et al. (2008), no significant difference in any region.
key_findings.note: The values listed for Kish et al. are that study's partial-volume-corrected figures, not the uncorrected values its abstract reports (occipital -46%, hippocampus -21%).

key_findings.finding: Five human studies of the 5-HT2A receptor divide 3 increases against 2 decreases, with abstinence ranging from 1.6 to 169.8 weeks, and no consistent relation between receptor binding and time since last use; the review concludes that these findings are inconsistent.

One animal and five human studies of the dopamine system found almost no effect: of three dopamine transporter studies, one reported striatal binding 13% higher than in polydrug controls (p=0.045, d=2.92) and 20% lower in people who also used amphetamines (p=0.007), and two found nothing; decarboxylase activity was 9% higher in the putamen than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021, d=1.10) but no different from polydrug controls; D2/3 binding and dopamine release did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Dopamine system' with Tables 8, 9 and 10; Discussion, 'Dopamine system'
key_findings.note: The authors of the transporter study read their own result as showing that amphetamine use, not MDMA, is associated with lower striatal dopamine transporter binding.

key_findings.finding: The review lists four explanations for lower binding that imaging cannot separate: down-regulation or internalization of the transporter, loss of the neurons expressing it, reduced protein expression, and competition from released neurotransmitter; and states that no PET or SPECT tracer directly assesses toxicity or degeneration.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 'Alteration in receptor binding and neurotoxicity'

key_findings.finding: On recovery, the review cites a baboon study (binding higher 40 days to 9 months after dosing in pons, midbrain and hypothalamus but still low in cortex), two SPECT and PET studies of people who had stopped, a positive correlation with abstinence, and the estimate that pallidostriatal binding returns to normal after about 200 days; it then asks whether recovered binding means functionally intact neurons and notes a study in which memory scores remained low although binding had normalized.

Its 'Current knowledge' box states that heavy use decreases transporter binding and that after 40 to 200 days binding recovers, that the dopamine system does not seem to be affected in humans, and that cannabis, cocaine and hallucinogen use do not seem to influence the transporter findings.

Limitations acknowledged by the authors: no imaging studies of systems other than serotonin and dopamine; small samples (animals 1 to 26, humans 14 to 116); some included studies required only 1 week of abstinence; varying tablet content over the years; and not all studies corrected for multiple comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 9 of 11 animal transporter studies found a significant loss; the Discussion says all 11 found lower binding and 10 reached significance.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two counts is wrong; the direction of the animal literature is not in doubt, but the figure quoted from this review depends on which sentence is read.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 lists partial-volume-corrected percentages for Kish et al. (2010) (hippocampus -31%, occipital -39%) although that study's primary outcome was the uncorrected measure (hippocampus -21%, occipital -46%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Anyone citing the review for that study's figures will quote the secondary analysis; the editors' claims should take such figures from the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentage changes are computed from binding values close to zero: for the prospective SPECT cohort the table gives occipital grey matter -40% from ratios of 0.05 against 0.03 in a study that found no significant difference anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader scanning the table sees a 40% reduction where the study reports a null result; the review flags the same problem for another study's 100% reductions but not here.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated range of human sample sizes, 14 to 116, does not match the review's own tables, in which the smallest human studies total 17 participants (10 and 7; 9 and 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the point that the studies are small stands.

reporting_issues.issue: One row of Table 4 describes its comparison group as polydrug controls in the sample column and as drug-naive controls in the outcome column.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which control group a difference refers to matters in this literature, as the review's own dopamine section shows; the row cannot be used without checking the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the three authors wrote several of the included studies, and the review neither says so nor weights its counts accordingly.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a conflict of interest in the declared sense, but the count of 14 of 16 includes studies by the reviewers themselves.
